title: Why did Neanderthals make string?
teaches: The four layers of any cloth (fibre, yarn, structure, finish), why twist holds fibres together, S and Z twist, and plying

parts.title: A scrap of cord on a stone tool

blocks.text: Abri du Maras is a rock shelter above the Ardèche valley in southern France. Neanderthals camped there on and off for tens of thousands of years, and left behind thousands of flaked stone tools. In 2020 a team led by the archaeologist Bruce Hardy published a close look at one of them, a pointed flake (a sharp chip struck from a larger stone) from a layer dated between 41,000 and 52,000 years ago. Stuck to its surface, under the microscope, was a scrap of cord about 6 mm long and half a millimetre thick.

The cord was made of fibres from the inner bark of a tree, probably a conifer (a cone-bearing tree such as a pine). The fibres had been gathered into three bundles, each bundle twisted in one direction, and then the three bundles twisted together in the opposite direction. That is the same construction as a modern three-strand rope. The layer it came from dates to a time when only Neanderthals lived in the region, so they are the likely makers. Whoever made it had worked out the two operations that every thread and rope since has depended on: twisting fibres into a yarn, and twisting yarns together into a stronger cord.[^maras]

Twisted fibre is older than farming, pottery or metal, and almost everything in this course is built from it. In this lesson we look at what twist does and why it works. Lesson 3 follows how people produced it in quantity, and the rest of the course follows what happened when they learned to produce it faster.

Every cloth can be described in four layers, and most confusion about fabric comes from mixing them up. The **fibre** is the raw material: cotton, wool, linen, silk, polyester. The **yarn** is fibre twisted into a continuous thread, and it can be thick or thin, tightly or loosely twisted, single or plied. The **structure** is how the yarn is put together into a flat sheet: woven (two sets of threads crossing at right angles), knitted (one thread pulled through itself in loops) or felted (fibres matted without spinning at all). The **finish** is everything done afterwards: dyeing, printing, brushing the surface into a nap, or coating it.

blocks.caption: Four independent choices. The same cotton fibre can become a stiff woven twill (denim) or a soft knit (a T-shirt); the same weave can be made of silk or polyester.

children.label: Tight or loose twist; single or plied

blocks.text: Many fabric names belong to one layer only. Satin is a structure, a weave in which long threads float across the surface; it can be woven from silk, polyester or cotton. Jersey is a knit. Denim is cotton woven in a diagonal pattern called twill, with only the lengthwise threads dyed blue (lesson 4 explains both terms). Fleece is usually a polyester knit brushed on one side to raise a soft surface of loose fibre ends, which is a fibre, a structure and a finish together. When a label says "100% cotton" it is describing only the first layer.

Most natural fibres are short. A cotton fibre is about 3 cm long, a wool fibre 5 to 15 cm. A thread long enough to weave or sew with has to be built from thousands of short fibres overlapping one another, and something has to stop them sliding apart when the thread is pulled. Glue is not the answer, since fibres do not stick to each other by themselves. A loose bundle of cotton fibres pulls apart with almost no force.

Twist turns each fibre into a spiral around the yarn's centre. When the yarn is pulled, every spiralling fibre is pulled straight, and a spiral that is pulled straight tightens inward, in the same way a rope wound round a post grips the post harder as the load on it increases. Each fibre squeezes the fibres inside it, and the fibres press against their neighbours, and friction between them resists sliding. The harder the yarn is pulled, the harder the fibres press together, which is why a well twisted yarn breaks its fibres before it lets them slip.

blocks.caption: A cotton yarn about a millimetre thick, hung with a weight. The bar shows the yarn's strength against the weight; on the right is a slack length of the same yarn.
blocks.task: Find a twist at which a single yarn holds the weight and still lies straight when slack

blocks.text: More twist is not always better. As the twist rises, the fibres run more across the yarn and less along it, so less of each fibre's own strength resists the pull, and past a certain point the yarn gets weaker. A highly twisted yarn is also **lively**: the twisted fibres are under strain and pull to untwist, so a slack length curls and snarls back on itself. Spinners choose a twist for each use. Warp yarn for a loom, which is held under tension for weeks, gets more twist. Yarn for soft knitwear gets less, because low twist leaves the fibres free to fluff out and trap air.

Twist can go in either of two directions, and textile archaeologists name them by letter. Hold a yarn upright. If its fibres slant like the middle stroke of a capital Z, rising to the right, it has **Z twist**. If they slant like the middle of an S, rising to the left, it has **S twist**. Neither is stronger. The direction depends on which way the spinner turned the spindle, and spinning traditions keep to one direction for centuries, so archaeologists use it as evidence of where a cloth was made. Most machine-spun yarn today is Z twisted.[^sz]

Two or more yarns twisted together make a **plied** yarn. The ply is put in the opposite direction to the singles: two Z singles are plied S. Each single is trying to untwist, and plying them the other way twists them back, so the two strains cancel and the plied yarn lies still. This is called a balanced yarn. Sewing thread, knitting wool and rope are all plied, and the Abri du Maras cord, with its three twisted bundles twisted together the other way, is a three-ply cord. In the figure above, switch to two plied singles at a high twist and the snarl disappears.

The textile historian Elizabeth Wayland Barber has argued that string deserves a place beside fire and stone tools among the oldest human technologies. She called its invention the **string revolution**. With cord, people could make snares and fishing lines, nets to catch animals and birds, bags and slings to carry food and babies, lashings to fix a stone point to a shaft, and eventually cloth. Most of these leave nothing behind, because plant fibre rots within a few years except in very dry, very wet or frozen ground. Cord like the Abri du Maras scrap survives only by luck.

So archaeologists piece the story together from indirect evidence. Small carved figures from Ice Age Europe, about 25,000 years old, show women wearing skirts made of hanging strings, carved in enough detail to show the twist; the best known is the Venus of Lespugue, from southwest France.[^lespugue] Pressed clay at Dolní Věstonice in the Czech Republic, of about the same age, carries the impressions of cords and of what may be woven or netted fabric. In Dzudzuana Cave in Georgia, a team reported in 2009 flax fibres more than 30,000 years old, some twisted and some apparently coloured, although other researchers have questioned whether the twist and the colours were made by people.[^lice]

**Try it.** Pull a tuft from a cotton wool ball and tug its ends: it comes apart with no effort. Now take a fresh tuft, pinch one end and roll the other between finger and thumb, always the same way, while drawing it out thin. In a minute you will have a short, uneven yarn that is far stronger than the tuft, and if you keep twisting and then let it go slack, it will kink back on itself. Fold it in half and let the two halves twist round each other: they ply themselves, in the opposite direction, and the kink is gone.

blocks.caption: Five questions on fibre, yarn and twist.

items.ask: A shop lists a scarf as "silk satin". What does each word describe?
choices: Silk is the fibre and satin is the weave structure
Silk is the weave and satin is the fibre
Both words name the fibre, in two languages
Silk is the finish and satin is the yarn
items.why: Silk is the raw material. Satin is a woven structure with long floating threads on its face, and it can be woven from silk, polyester or cotton.

items.ask: Why does a bundle of untwisted cotton fibres pull apart easily, while the same fibres twisted into yarn do not?
choices: Twist makes each fibre spiral, so a pull presses the fibres together and friction stops them sliding
Twist melts the fibres' waxy coating so that they stick together
Twist makes the fibres longer, so they overlap more
Twist glues the fibres together with their own natural oils
items.why: Short fibres hold only by friction. A spiral pulled straight tightens inward, so the harder the yarn is pulled, the harder the fibres press against each other.

items.ask: A spinner keeps adding twist to a single yarn, far beyond what it needs. What happens?
choices: It gets weaker and snarls when slack, because the fibres run across it and strain to untwist
It keeps getting stronger, so the most twisted yarn is always best
Nothing changes once the fibres stop slipping
It turns into a plied yarn by itself
items.why: Past a moderate twist the fibres lie more across the yarn than along it, so less of their strength resists a pull, and the stored twist makes a slack length kink.

items.ask: Two Z-twisted singles are to be plied into a balanced yarn that lies straight. Which way should the ply go?
choices: S, the opposite way, so each single's urge to untwist is cancelled
Z, the same way, to add more twist
Either way; direction makes no difference to plying
No ply twist at all; the singles are laid side by side
items.why: Plying in the opposite direction twists the singles back against their own twist, so the strains cancel. Two Z singles are plied S.

items.ask: Cord more than 40,000 years old is very rarely found. What is the main reason?
choices: Plant fibre rots within years except in very dry, wet or frozen ground
People did not make cord until about 10,000 years ago
Early cord was made only of animal sinew, which dissolves
Archaeologists only began looking for cord in 2020
items.why: Fibre decays fast, so even common objects rarely survive. The Abri du Maras scrap survived because it was stuck to a stone tool, and most early evidence is indirect: carvings, clay impressions and tools.

summary: **Four layers.** Every cloth is a fibre, twisted into yarn, built into a structure (woven, knitted or felted), then finished (dyed, printed, brushed).
**Names belong to layers.** Satin is a weave, jersey is a knit, denim is a cotton twill; "100% cotton" names only the fibre.
**Twist holds by friction.** Spiralling fibres press together when the yarn is pulled, so short fibres can make an endless thread.
**There is a best twist.** Too little and fibres slip; too much and the yarn weakens and snarls when slack.
**S and Z.** Twist goes one of two ways, named by the slant of the letters, and traditions keep to one, which helps date and place a cloth.
**Plying balances.** Singles twisted together the opposite way cancel each other's strain, as in rope, sewing thread and the Abri du Maras cord.
**String is very old.** Cord at least 41,000 years old, most likely made by Neanderthals, used the same three-ply construction as modern rope.

maras.title: How the cord was dated and identified
maras.text: The cord itself was not dated; the layer it lay in was, by several methods, to between 41,000 and 52,000 years ago, when only Neanderthals lived in the region. The fibres were identified from their cell structure under the microscope as inner bark, most likely of a conifer. The study was published by Bruce Hardy and colleagues in Scientific Reports in 2020.

sz.title: Spindles and twist direction
sz.text: A spinner who rolls a spindle down the thigh with the right hand usually produces one direction and a left-handed roll the other, so direction partly reflects how a tradition held its tools. Ancient Egyptian linen is mostly S twisted, for example, while most European wool of the same period is Z twisted.

lice.title: Clothing older than string
lice.text: Clothes themselves are older than any cord we have. Body lice live in clothing, not hair, and split from head lice when people began wearing clothes; a 2011 genetic study by Melissa Toups and colleagues dated that split to at least 83,000 years ago, and perhaps 170,000. Those first clothes were probably hides, sewn or tied.

lespugue.title: The string skirt
lespugue.text: String skirts worn low on the hips appear on carved figures from France to Russia, and Barber notes that very similar skirts were still worn as a sign of a married or marriageable woman in parts of eastern Europe in the 19th century. Whether the two are connected over 20,000 years is unknown.
